# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)

- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).

- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

screens.why5: The belief Keel wrote keeps "the job runs first time, no resubmits" but drops my second benefit, the shorter wait in the queue, so the screen holds only half of what I typed.
screens.instead: Keep the same question, and carry both benefits into the belief: "For most, their last job would have gone better with it: it runs first time with no resubmits, and it waits less in the queue."

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than today's way, Keel shows me the benefits it drew from that and asks me to check them, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Runs first time, no resubmits and a shorter wait in the queue are exactly how a researcher on a SLURM cluster talks about a job.
screens.why3: Every researcher on a shared cluster knows from their own last job whether it failed and was resubmitted and how long it sat in the queue.
screens.why4: Both rows are real and distinct, but the line-level code fixes and debugging failures in seconds rather than days are missing, and the test leans on the first row alone.
screens.why5: The rows keep my fewer attempts and shorter queue wait, but the tested belief claims most last jobs would have gone better, when for many over-requesters the job ran fine and only the cluster wasted capacity.
screens.instead: Rows: The job runs first time, no resubmits / A shorter wait in the queue / Finds why a job failed in minutes, not days

screens.why1: After what it does better, asking what researchers must change to start using it is the obvious next question about adoption.
screens.why2: "They" and the hint's "setup" pull me toward the operator installing the agent on every node, while the question is about the researcher, who installs nothing and only changes how they size and fix jobs.
screens.why3: I know exactly what a researcher has to do differently: take the predicted sizes instead of padding two to three times, and apply the line-level fixes.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, "Leave this out of the study", and it fits a free-text belief I could choose not to test.
screens.why5: Keel's belief keeps "use the suggested sizes instead of padding" but drops my second step, applying the line-level code fixes, and adds a "most would" forecast I didn't type.
screens.instead: What will researchers have to do differently when they submit a job? (e.g. take the suggested memory, GPUs and walltime instead of padding; apply the code fixes it flags)

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'd have to do to start, Keel hands back the two steps for me to check and picks the one to test, the last of the four solution beliefs.
screens.why2: Padding a request and line-level code fixes are how researchers and I talk about submissions; only the intro repeating the title is a small stumble.
screens.why3: Whether a researcher would trust a predicted size over their own padding is the core of what I know about my users.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and are the two things a researcher actually has to do, since the agent install is the operator's job, not theirs.
screens.why5: The rows and the belief keep my words, using the suggested sizes instead of padding as the tested step, with nothing added or bent.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the two efforts Keel wrote from my answer, it asks which one is the real risk, which is the obvious next step before the stranger test is fixed.
screens.why2: 'Suggested sizes' and 'padding' are exactly how I and the researchers on our clusters talk about over-requesting memory, GPUs and walltime, so it reads in one pass.
screens.why3: I know from the pilots and the thread that trusting our sizes over their own margin is the hard part, while the code fixes are optional, so I can answer this from what I see.
screens.why4: The two options are the two efforts I named, distinct and in my words, and with only two to choose between, no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: The belief 'Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding' is my own adoption claim, and the one-in-three bar fits how I would judge it.

screens.why1: My go-to-market is a free two-week measurement and then a paid pilot, so being asked whether to collect pilot sign-ups just before the study goes out is the obvious last step.
screens.why2: 'Offer a pilot?' with the exact line respondents will see and where I find the yeses is plain on first reading.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads is my own call; I'm onboarding paid pilots right now.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, but my pilot is installed by the cluster's operator, not an individual researcher, so the option I'd actually want is missing: ask only the operators in Part 3.
screens.why5: The screen adds nothing about my product or roles and keeps my intent, though 'try this for real' fits a cluster-wide install by the operator less well than it fits a researcher.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? — Yes, ask the cluster operators ("Would you run a two-week waste measurement on your cluster? Leave your email.") / Yes, ask everyone / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions is the natural last setup step before the study goes out to researchers.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, typing, credits, recording and text-message delivery into one paragraph, so it needs a second read.
screens.why3: Picking a voice from two five-second samples is something I can do on the spot.
screens.why4: Two named voices with samples are distinct and complete, but the typed answer speaks of a face while the hint speaks only of a voice, so it is unclear whether I am picking a voice, a face or both.
screens.why5: Nothing of my idea is restated here, and 'researchers' is my own word for who gets asked.
screens.instead: Who should ask researchers your questions on video? Hear each and pick one (400 credits either way): Daphne ▶ 5 s / Saskia ▶ 5 s

screens.why1: Once I've said who asks my researchers the questions, choosing how they answer is the obvious next thing before I send the link.
screens.why2: The three choices are clear, but 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' made me read twice, since it could mean Daphne is busy recording interviews rather than that her video is still being made.
screens.why3: I know my researchers: they're at a terminal between job submissions and would sooner tap through quickly than talk to a video, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: Video AI, read and tap, and let them choose are distinct and cover the real choices, and the readiness note on each tells me what I'd be waiting for.
screens.why5: It calls them researchers as I typed it and leaks nothing about Expanse or the operators.
screens.instead: How should researchers answer? — AI interviewer Daphne (asks aloud on video; her video is still being made, ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap (ready now) / Let them choose (ready when Daphne's video is)

screens.why1: Sending is the last step, so after choosing how researchers answer, the obvious next question is who receives the link.
screens.why2: Named people, a Keel contact list, or one open link posted where researchers already are (a cluster's user Slack or mailing list) are all clear to me on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly whom I'd reach: researchers I can name at the HPC centres and labs we've talked to, or a post in a cluster's user channel.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I'd actually recruit, and nothing obvious is missing.
screens.why5: My pick of named people is kept, and nothing of Expanse leaks into the choice.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits under the title, and each card gives the deciding number beside it: '4 answered · 5 needed to call it'.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart, and the tally '3 too few · 7 people answered' needs a second look: it doesn't say why 7 answered but only 4 count on each card, and it never says 5 is the bar.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry the exact belief lines I checked, though Keel's statement above them garbles my mechanism ('the researcher installed on every node').
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need one more usable answer per belief, but the screen never tells me to send to more researchers or how many more.
screens.why_b5: Nothing is claimed beyond the data; each card keeps n=4 visible and declines to call any belief.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 7 researchers answered, but only 4 reached these questions (3 stopped at the gate), and each belief needs 5. Send the study to about 3 more researchers on 100+ GPU clusters to get a call.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right next to '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no verdict yet and which number decides that.
screens.why_b2: Yes 3, with some steps 1 and No 0 are plain, but 'against your bar · 3 of 4' with the marker at 3 and a ghost cell made me stop: I had to work out that 3 of 4 is my bar, not the result, and that the ghost is the missing fifth person.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and 'For most researchers, the source code sat on the cluster' are exactly the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it doesn't tell me that all four counted answers lean my way, or that one more countable answer (or Rafael's, made concrete) would settle it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible throughout, Rafael's guess is excluded and named, and 'a lean, not a call' keeps a 4-of-4 from being sold as a hold.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted, 5 needed', and the So line repeats both without contradiction.
screens.why_b2: What is counted (better vs same) and the 4 people are plain, but the bar labelled 'your bar · 3 of 4' next to 'no more than 1 in 3 say no difference or worse' mixes a count with a ceiling, and the ghost cell for Rafael takes a second look to place.
screens.why_b3: The title Relative advantage and the line 'For most, their last job would have gone better with it: the job runs first time, no resubmits.' are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' tells me not to act but not what to do; it never says one more counted researcher would decide it, or that 3 of 4 is currently leaning my way.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible throughout, the small group is named as 'a lean, not a call', Rafael's guess is excluded and said why, and the 3 of 4 lean is never dressed up as a held belief.

screens.why_b1: 'Too few to call' sits beside 4 against 5 needed, but the verdict line says '4 answered' while the count line says '5 answered · 4 counted', so I have to work out that the deciding number is the counted four, not the answers.
screens.why_b2: Two plain Yes, two conditional Yes, nothing against, out of 4 counted, with the bar marker at 3 of 4, reads at once.
screens.why_b3: 'Adoption friction' and 'Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding' are the words I checked.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' tells me what not to conclude but not what to do: get one more counted answer, or re-ask Rafael for his actual last job, and note that half the yeses hinge on the sizes being clearly worth it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know where it stands and why.
screens.why_b3: 'Relative advantage' and 'For most, their last job would have gone better with it: the job runs first time, no resubmits.' are exactly the dimension and line I checked.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next: no line saying to send the study to more researchers, and no note that one 'no difference' already uses up most of the one-in-three allowance with only four answers in.

screens.why1: As the first screen it obviously checks that I submit jobs to a big GPU cluster before asking about my last job, which is exactly the gate this study needs.
screens.why2: Jobs, cluster and GPUs are my everyday words, and I can answer it on one read.
screens.why3: I know our cluster is big, but I'd be estimating whether it is over 100 GPUs, since I see my partition and queue, not the whole node count.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers a gate question, and the guidelines give a gate no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but it drops the founder's 'shared' cluster and the last-five-working-days window, so someone with a private box or who hasn't submitted lately still passes.
screens.why6: One short question with two options that say cleanly; 'a hundred' says fine.
screens.instead: In the last week, did you submit a job to a shared cluster of about 100 GPUs or more? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I'm on a big cluster, asking whether a job of mine ran out of what I asked for in the last week is the obvious next step, and it leads straight into the story.
screens.why2: "Resource limit" makes me stop and think: does it mean the job got killed for running out of memory or wall time, or just ran close to it? I'd say "got OOM-killed or hit walltime".
screens.why3: I know exactly whether one of my jobs died on memory or time this week, because I'm the one who resubmits it.
screens.why4: A gate should carry no escape, but this one shows two chips, and "I'd rather not say" is one that shouldn't exist at all, so the chips don't fit.
screens.why5: The founder's point is having to guess memory, GPUs and time before submitting, but this asks only about the under-guess, so someone who padded every request and wasted the cluster says no and is screened out.
screens.why6: Said aloud it's one short question ending in "Yes or no," which I can answer on first hearing.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a job of yours get killed for running out of memory, GPUs or time? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said a job hit its limit this week, it makes sense to show me the idea before asking what I think of it.
screens.why2: Walltime, SLURM, Kubernetes and GPU memory are my everyday words, but 'every node of your own network' is off, since I'd say 'on our cluster', and 'line-level optimisations' makes me stop and wonder what it would actually change in my code.
screens.why3: Guessing GPU memory and walltime at submit, and losing days when a fine-tuning run gets killed, is exactly my week.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: It reads as a deliberate idea card and keeps the founder's meaning, predicting what a job needs at submit and explaining failures, with no stray terms about me as a user or buyer.
screens.why6: Heard once, the 'how' runs five sentences instead of one line, 'line-level optimisations' is a mouthful, and the belief repeats 'GPU memory, memory, CPUs and walltime' instead of pointing back, so it is too long to hold.
screens.instead: Imagine Expanse, a tool that predicts what each job needs before you submit it. It runs on your cluster with SLURM or Kubernetes, reads your code, script and hardware, and at submit tells you the GPU memory, memory, CPUs and walltime to ask for; if a job fails, it says why and how to fix it. The people building it believe those predictions would match what the job really needs and catch failures before they happen.

screens.why1: A compatibility check right after the idea card is plausible, but where my code lives has little obvious link to predicting a job's memory, GPUs and run time.
screens.why2: I know what it means, but 'sit on the cluster' is not how I'd say it; I'd say the code was on the cluster or in my home dir or repo there.
screens.why3: I know exactly where my fine-tuning code lived for my last job.
screens.why4: 'Yes, with some steps' is odd for a where-is-it fact, since code is either on the cluster or pulled in by a container or git clone at submit.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but the founder likely meant whether the tool could read my job script and code, and 'source code sat on the cluster' drifts from that.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and three options I can hold on one hearing.
screens.instead: Think of your last job. Could a tool on the cluster read your job script and code before it ran? Yes; yes, with some setup; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the check that it would work with my setup, asking whether it would have helped my last job is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: I know what a job is, but 'go better' is vague: it could mean not getting OOM-killed, starting sooner in the queue, or not hogging GPUs I didn't need, so I'd have to pick a meaning.
screens.why3: I remember my last job, what I requested and whether it died or sat idle, so I can judge this from my own run.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it cleanly, and 'I can't tell' fits for a prediction tool I haven't seen.
screens.why5: It names the idea as the card did, predicted resources per job, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms reaches me.
screens.why6: One short question with four short options I can hold after hearing them once, and the escape said last.
screens.instead: Would Expanse have helped the job that hit its resource limit finish without wasting the cluster, or not? A lot · A little · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after asking whether Expanse would have helped, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually give up padding to use it, since that is the real cost for me.
screens.why2: Padding my requests is exactly how I'd put it, but 'suggested sizes' made me pause, because I think of memory, GPUs and wall time as requests, not sizes.
screens.why3: I pad every submission because under-requesting kills a run and loses days, so I know exactly whether I'd trust a predicted number instead.
screens.why4: My real condition isn't whether it's 'clearly worth it' but whether it has proven it won't get my job killed, and there's no middle option like 'only for short or cheap jobs'.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea of swapping padded requests for predicted ones, in words I use myself, and nothing beyond the shown idea leaks.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four short options and one escape, easy to hold after hearing it once.
screens.instead: To use Expanse, you'd request what it predicts instead of padding. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Yes, once it proved right on a few runs · Only for short or cheap jobs · No · I can't tell
